source: Checking Equations with Units
Every term in a physics equation must have the same units, which catches many mistakes before they happen.
Students add quantities with different units, or keep an answer whose units show the formula was misremembered.

In Dimensional Analysis you used units to convert from one unit to another, letting the units you didn't want cancel. Physics uses the same habit for a second job: checking equations. Before you trust a formula, or an answer, look at its units.
Units multiply, divide and cancel just like algebra. Every term that is added, subtracted or set equal in an equation must have the same units. If they don't match, the equation is wrong.

An equation says two amounts are the same quantity. A length can equal a length, but it can never equal a time, just as 3 meters can't be "the same as" 3 seconds. Adding works the same way: $3\ \text{m} + 2\ \text{s}$ has no meaning, so any formula that asks you to do it must be misremembered.
Units you will meet in this course. Newtons and joules are shorthand for combinations of kg, m and s.
Worked examples
Check the units of $x = v_0 t + \tfrac12 a t^2$.
Checking a motion equation
The units match: m = m + m.
Left side: $x$ is a position, in m.
First term: $v_0 t$ has units $\dfrac{\text{m}}{\text{s}} \cdot \text{s} = \text{m}$.
Second term: $\tfrac12$ has no units, so $a t^2$ has units $\dfrac{\text{m}}{\text{s}^2} \cdot \text{s}^2 = \text{m}$.
Every term is in meters, so the equation passes the test.
A student remembers the speed of a falling object as $v = 2gh$. Is that possible?
Catching a slip
No. It must be $v = \sqrt{2gh}$.
Units of $2gh$: $\dfrac{\text{m}}{\text{s}^2} \cdot \text{m} = \dfrac{\text{m}^2}{\text{s}^2}$.
A speed is in $\dfrac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}$, so the two sides don't match.
Taking a square root fixes the units: $\sqrt{\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2} = \text{m/s}$. The real formula is $v = \sqrt{2gh}$.
You compute $\dfrac{v^2}{a}$ with $v$ in m/s and $a$ in m/s². What kind of quantity did you find?
Units of an answer
A length, in meters (it shows up later as a stopping distance).
$\dfrac{(\text{m/s})^2}{\text{m/s}^2} = \dfrac{\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2}{\text{m}/\text{s}^2}$.
The $\text{s}^2$ cancel, and $\text{m}^2/\text{m} = \text{m}$.

Adding quantities with different units, or keeping an answer whose units don't fit the question. If you are asked for a distance and your answer comes out in m/s, you used the wrong formula or dropped a factor of time. Quick check: write the units next to every number as you work, and look at the units of the final answer before you look at its size.
Matching units can't catch a missing $\tfrac12$ or a wrong factor of 2, because plain numbers have no units. Units prove an equation wrong; they can't prove it right.
